title: Physics-Guided Motion Loss for Video Generation Model
claim: Our method computes spectral motion losses from generated output and feeds them back, adaptively combined, to train a pretrained model.
layout: 1 row, left-to-right, three parallel branches, feedback arrow loops back, legend right
description: A single horizontal flow diagram. At far left a large gray box labeled 'Video generation mode[l]' (pretrained network) sends an arrow into a green rounded box 'Low-frequency DFT Transform (0-0.3)'. From it three arrows fan out to three stacked green rectangles: Translational Motion Loss (L_trans), Rotational Motion Loss (L_rot) and Scaling Motion Loss (L_scale). These converge into a tall green 'Adaptive Weight' box, then into a 'Motion Loss (L_motion)' box. A thin blue line from the final box runs up and back over the top to the video generator, showing the training feedback loop. A legend at right explains gray as 'Pretrained network' and green as 'Loss compute module'. Dark blue arrows and a pale green and gray palette keep it clean, and the eye follows left to right.
caption: Our pipeline. From the generated video, we compute a low-pass 3D FFT, feed the spectral features to three motion losses (translation, rotation, scaling), and adaptively combine them into $\mathcal{L}_{motion}$ for training.
abstract: Current video diffusion models generate visually compelling content but often violate basic laws of physics, producing subtle artifacts like rubber-sheet deformations and inconsistent object motion. We introduce a frequency-domain physics prior that improves motion plausibility without modifying model architectures. Our method decomposes common rigid motions (translation, rotation, scaling) into lightweight spectral losses, requiring only 2.7% of frequency coefficients while preserving 97%+ of spectral energy. Applied to Open-Sora, MVDIT, and Hunyuan, our approach improves both motion accuracy and action recognition by ~11% on average on OpenVID-1M (relative), while maintaining visual quality. User studies show 74--83% preference for our physics-enhanced videos. It also reduces warping error by 22--37% (depending on the backbone) and improves temporal consistency scores. These results indicate that simple, global spectral cues are an effective drop-in regularizer for physically plausible motion in video diffusion.
